title: Palm Beach County’s Israel Bonds Holdings Hit 24% of Portfolio Last Month
author: Waqas Ahmed
content:

bd5c-4ceb-b753-6e0d6ae296e2_3000x2000.jpeg)A Palm Beach Sheriff's Office
deputy attempts to remove Nihaya Atchanah during the public comments portion
during a Palm Beach County Board of County Commissioners meeting in downtown

Palm Beach County, Florida, the world's largest government investor in Israeli
government bonds, held nearly a quarter of its investment portfolio in Israeli
bonds before $67.5 million of the securities matured on November 1, far
exceeding its own investment limits. The county did not reinvest the proceeds
because its existing holdings were already above the permitted ceiling,
according to its interim comptroller. The repayment reduced the county's
exposure but left 22.5% of its portfolio invested in Israeli government debt,
still above the allowed investment cap of 15%.

The investments had prompted months of protests by residents, who have also
faced arrests and removal from public meetings while attempting to challenge
the county's financial support for Israel.

At a September 15 budget hearing, Palestinian American legal scholar and human
rights attorney Noura Erakat was [arrested and
charged](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/16/noura-erakat-
palestinian-arrested-florida) with misdemeanor trespassing after refusing
orders to leave the chamber. Sheriff's deputies also removed other attendees
who had sought to speak against the investments. County officials had limited
public comment to one minute per speaker and ruled discussion of Israel bonds
outside the scope of the budget hearing. Erakat and civil rights organizations
condemned the arrest as an infringement on free speech, while county officials
maintained that investment policy was not on the hearing's agenda.

Lydia Ghuman, executive director of the Internationalist Law Center, accused
county officials of using vague public-comment rules to suppress opposition to
the investments. The rules allow officials to curtail comments for conduct
deemed "disruptive" or that "obstructs the meeting progress," language that
officials use to target criticism of Israel bonds, Ghuman said. "They now use
this as grounds to ensure you can be taken away by the sheriff and the
microphone silenced," she told Drop Site.

post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb5dc4fd4-ea45-42cd-
ae3a-05a91d098f55_588x365.jpeg)Former Palm Beach County Clerk Michael Caruso
announces another round of Israel bond investments, pushing the total to $1
billion or 17% of the county total investment portfolio, on January 7, 2026.
USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect.

Interim Clerk and Comptroller Shannon Ramsey-Chessman, who assumed the
position after the former County Clerk Michael Caruso was suspended following
his August [arrest](https://www.miamiherald.com/news/politics-
government/state-politics/article317511449.html) on child sexual abuse
charges, confirmed in a statement to Drop Site News that Israeli government
bonds represented 24.2% of the county's investment portfolio immediately
before November 1, falling to 22.5% after the $67.5 million maturity. Caruso
has pleaded not guilty to the child sex abuse charges.

"Because we will continue to be at the policy's maximum allowable investment
percentage after the maturity of $67.5 million in bonds on November 1, we are
not permitted to reinvest at this time," Ramsey-Chessman told Drop Site in an
earlier statement. "However, we will review reinvesting once we may do so
within the compliance cap."

The last development in the Palm Beach divestment fight comes amid a growing
national campaign to withdraw public money from investments connected to
Israel. In Providence, Rhode Island, more than 76% of voters on November 3
[approved](https://rhodeislandcurrent.com/2026/11/03/providence-voters-
overwhelmingly-approve-divestment-measure/) a ballot measure requiring the
city "to divest from countries and companies profiting from genocide,
apartheid, ethnic cleansing, and prolonged military occupation." Organizers
describe it as the first binding municipal divestment law approved directly by
voters.

In Massachusetts, Cambridge's city council
[voted](https://csindie.com/cambridge-votes-5-4-for-order-to-divest-money-
from-businesses-involved-with-israel/) on October 28 to divest $24 million in
municipal funds from companies associated with apartheid and genocide, while
Easthampton's council unanimously adopted a divestment resolution on October
22. Somerville is scheduled to consider a binding boycott and divestment
ordinance on November 12, following voter approval of a divestment ballot
question last year.

More than 30 U.S. cities, counties, and states have taken divestment measures
over the past three years, according to the Internationalist Law Center.

"These divestment wins across the country signal that Israel bonds, and
genocide, are in fact poor investments that harm taxpayers," said Ghuman.

The county's holdings, which reached approximately $1 billion in January, fell
to roughly $932.5 million following the repayment, assuming no other changes
in principal. But the new figures raise questions about how Palm Beach County
came to hold such a large concentration of public funds in Israeli government
debt, even as officials repeatedly sought to increase the limits governing
those investments.

Ramsey-Chessman defended the county's investment practices, saying the clerk's
office had always evaluated investments according to three factors: safety,
liquidity, and rate of return.

"Our previous investments in Israel Bonds were focused on the significant
investment income for county taxpayers, at a time when other investment
opportunities were not performing at the same level," she said.

The county's repeated efforts to increase the investment ceiling have also
raised questions about whether the investments were motivated solely by
financial considerations.

The investments expanded under former Clerk and Comptroller Joseph Abruzzo,
who publicly described them as reflecting the county's commitment to Israel.

Ramsey-Chessman attributed the unusually high percentage of Israel bonds in
the portfolio to changes in the county's investment policy and seasonal
fluctuations in the amount of money available for investment.

"Keep in mind that when we made our last purchase in March, the allowable cap
was 18%, and we invested up to that cap," Ramsey-Chessman said.

The county receives most of its property tax revenue in late November and
December, she explained, leaving its investment portfolio at its lowest point
of the year before those payments arrive. As the overall portfolio shrinks,
Israel bonds account for a larger percentage of its value, even without
additional purchases, according to the interim comptroller.

## "Not Really Good Practice"

Tom Sgouros, a municipal finance expert, said seasonal fluctuations in tax
revenues are predictable, but the larger concern is the county's concentration
of investments in a single issuer. "It's not really good practice to hold a
quarter of your investment portfolio in one investment, period," he told Drop
Site News. "Diversification does not mean buying different bond issues from
the same issuer."

The county's investment policy measures the allowable percentage of Israel
bonds at the time of purchase. That means a subsequent increase in their share
of the portfolio does not necessarily constitute a violation of the purchase
restriction. Nevertheless, the figures show that nearly a quarter of the
county's investment portfolio was concentrated in Israeli government debt
before the November repayment, a level substantially above the current ceiling
intended to limit such exposure.

An [investigation](https://follow-the-money-ffb82d.beehiiv.com/p/palm-beach-
county-bought-israel-bonds-over-its-own-cap) by Colby Donovan published last
month revealed that Palm Beach County exceeded its own investment limits when
purchasing Israel bonds on three occasions since January 2024. On January 6,
2026, the county purchased $350.5 million in Israeli government bonds,
bringing its holdings to $1 billion, or 20.04% of its investment portfolio,
despite an 18% cap. The investigation, based on county trade records and
custodian reports, found that the county exceeded its allowable allocation by
approximately $101.7 million. It also found that the county's automated
compliance checks did not monitor Israel bonds as a percentage of the overall
portfolio.

In October 2025, the county commission approved a temporary increase in the
allowable Israel bonds allocation from 15% to 18%, permitting further
purchases before the limit was scheduled to revert to 15%. In February, the
county's Investment Policy Committee considered making the higher ceiling
permanent. That proposal failed in a 3-3 vote, although the committee approved
a temporary extension of the 18% limit through March 2.

Last month, Palm Beach residents and organizers said they had persuaded two
members of the county's Investment Policy Committee to [vote
against](https://www.palmbeachpost.com/story/news/local/2026/10/19/israel-
bond-cap-stays-put-despite-67-5-million-set-to-mature/92286713007/?gnt-
cfr=1&gca-cat=p&gca-uir=false&gca-
epti=z116701p119350l003050c119350e009375v116701&gca-ft=60&gca-ds=sophi) a
proposal to increase the allotment to 20%. Campaign organizers met with
Ramsey-Chessman and her staff on October 15 to present their objections to the
investments.

But the November non-reinvestment was not a discretionary divestment decision.
Ramsey-Chessman said the existing investment cap prohibited the clerk's office
from purchasing additional Israel bonds, regardless of the campaign's demands.
The October 15 committee vote had
[preserved](https://www.aol.com/articles/county-committee-
keeps-15-cap-090812000.html) that restriction by rejecting a proposal to raise
the cap from 15% to 20%.

The county is scheduled to receive repayments on four additional occasions:
January 2027, February 2027, March 2027, and August 2028. If those payments
are also allowed to mature without reinvestment, the county could eventually
eliminate its entire portfolio.

The November repayment came just two days before voters[
elected](https://www.sun-sentinel.com/2026/11/03/suspended-palm-beach-county-
clerk-loses-election-to-democrat-challenger-drucker/) Democrat Yvette Drucker,
a former Boca Raton deputy mayor, as the county's new clerk and comptroller.
Drucker defeated Michael Caruso, the suspended incumbent.

Drucker, who was scheduled to take office November 10,[
campaigned](https://www.orlandosentinel.com/2026/11/03/suspended-palm-beach-
county-clerk-loses-election-to-democrat-challenger-drucker/) on maintaining
the county's investments in Israel bonds, but has also said she would evaluate
investments based on financial considerations rather than political or
ideological tests. She will oversee future investment decisions involving the
county's remaining holdings.

Palm Beach residents, including Palestinian Americans whose family members
were killed or displaced in Gaza, challenged the county's investments in
Israel bonds, arguing in a lawsuit that local public money should not finance
the Israeli government and that officials were making investment decisions for
political rather than financial reasons.

The residents' legal challenge was dismissed in July, when Palm Beach County
Circuit Judge Glenn Kelley ruled that the plaintiffs had not established
sufficient grounds to bring a taxpayer lawsuit. Their attorneys
[appealed](https://newsletter.mariannedhenin.com/organizers-aim-to-thwart-
purchase-of-israel-bonds-by-worlds-largest-investor/) in late August.

"Our tax dollars are supposed to be used for the benefit of our own community,
and I believe that the Comptroller did not have our community's best interest
in mind when he made these investments," one of the plaintiffs, identified in
court documents as Jane Doe, said in a sworn declaration.
